t: Section 534 of title 28, United States Code, is amended by striking subsection (e)(3)(B) and inserting the following: “(B) the term ‘protection order’ includes—“(i) any injunction, restraining order, or any other order issued by a civil or criminal court for the purpose of preventing violent or threatening acts or harassment against, sexual violence or contact or communication with or physical proximity to, another person, including any temporary or final orders issued by civil or criminal courts whether obtained by filing an independent action or as a pendente lite order in another proceeding so long as any civil order was issued in response to a complaint, petition, or motion filed by or on behalf of a person seeking protection; and “(ii) any support, child custody or visitation provisions, orders, remedies, or relief issued as part of a protection order, restraining order, or stay away injunction pursuant to State, tribal, territorial, or local law authorizing the issuance of protection orders, restraining orders, or injunctions for the protection of victims of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking.”.

fable.w: This section only amends the definition of 'protection order' in 28 U.S.C. 534. The tempting reading is that the words 'complaint, petition, or motion' and the references to State, tribal, and local law signal outside-party involvement, but they merely describe the court orders covered by the definition. No outside party is consulted on, or given a right to challenge, any federal decision.
fable.s: so long as any civil order was issued in response to a complaint, petition, or motion filed by or on behalf of a person seeking protection

qwen_block.w: This section defines the term 'protection order' for the purposes of Title 28 of the U.S. Code. It describes legal orders issued by courts (civil or criminal) and does not establish a process for the federal government to consult with or coordinate with outside parties before making a federal decision. The mention of 'complaint, petition, or motion filed by... a person seeking protection' refers to the initiation of a judicial proceeding, not participation in a federal administrative or policy decision. Therefore, it does not meet the definition of participation.
qwen_block.s: the term ‘protection order’ includes—(i) any injunction, restraining order, or any other order issued by a civil or criminal court for the purpose of preventing violent or threatening acts or harassment against, sexual violence or contact or communication with or physical proximity to, another person, including any temporary or final orders issued by civil or criminal courts whether obtained by filing an independent action or as a pendente lite order in another proceeding so long as any civil order was issued in response to a complaint, petition, or motion filed by or on behalf of a person seeking protection; and (ii) any support, child custody or visitation provisions, orders, remedies, or relief issued as part of a protection order, restraining order, or stay away injunction pursuant to State, tribal, territorial, or local law authorizing the issuance of protection orders, restraining orders, or injunctions for the protection of victims of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

opus.w: This amendment only redefines 'protection order' for 28 U.S.C. § 534. It creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with outside parties, or right to challenge a federal decision. The 'petition' mentioned is a private filing in a civil or criminal court asking for a protection order, so it is not part of any federal decision. The keyword alone does not make this participation.
opus.s: so long as any civil order was issued in response to a complaint, petition, or motion filed by or on behalf of a person seeking protection
opus.b: 1. **Tempting but wrong reading:** The section mentions a "complaint, petition, or motion filed by or on behalf of a person seeking protection," which sounds like an outside party taking part in a decision. That reading fails. Those filings ask a state, tribal or local court for a protection order. They don't bring anyone into a federal agency's decision. The section only changes how "protection order" is defined in 28 U.S.C. § 534.

qwen_chat.w: This section defines the term 'protection order' for federal legal purposes. It describes orders issued by state, tribal, or local courts but does not require the federal government to consult with or coordinate with these outside entities before making a federal decision. The definition is substantive, not procedural, regarding federal decision-making processes.
qwen_chat.s: Section 534 of title 28, United States Code, is amended by striking subsection (e)(3)(B) and inserting the following: “(B) the term ‘protection order’ includes—“(i) any injunction, restraining order, or any other order issued by a civil or criminal court for the purpose of preventing violent or threatening acts or harassment against, sexual violence or contact or communication with or physical proximity to, another person, including any temporary or final orders issued by civil or criminal courts whether obtained by filing an independent action or as a pendente lite order in another proceeding so long as any civil order was issued in response to a complaint, petition, or motion filed by or on behalf of a person seeking protection; and “(ii) any support, child custody or visitation provisions, orders, remedies, or relief issued as part of a protection order, restraining order, or stay away injunction pursuant to State, tribal, territorial, or local law authorizing the issuance of protection orders, restraining orders, or injunctions for the protection of victims of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault, or stalking.”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that because the definition of "protection order" includes orders issued by state, tribal, or local courts, this implies participation by those entities. The involvement of state/tribal/local courts is descriptive of the source of the order, not a procedural requirement for federal decision-making involving outside parties.
